questions.explanation: This is the clearest possible illustration of the difference this level is teaching between legitimate philosophical schools and heresy: both Scotus and Aquinas affirm the same revealed truths about God and creation, and both are honored figures in the Church's tradition, but they explain the metaphysics of that truth differently. Disagreement here is a live philosophical question, not a doctrinal fracture.
questions.hint: Ask whether both thinkers still affirm the same revealed truths -- they do; they just explain the metaphysics differently.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, n. 44 (1998)

questions.prompt: St. Bonaventure and the Franciscan tradition emphasized a theory of divine ______ -- that the human mind grasps intelligible truth only with God's direct illuminating assistance -- in contrast to the more Aristotelian, sense-based account of knowledge Aquinas developed.
questions.correctAnswer: illumination
questions.explanation: Augustinian illumination theory holds that the mind cannot reach unchanging truth by its own natural power alone; it needs a special divine light. Aquinas's more Aristotelian account instead grounds knowledge in abstraction from sense experience, with a much lighter role for direct divine assistance in ordinary knowing. Both remain live, fully Catholic positions.
questions.hint: The word describes divine light making truth graspable to the mind.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, n. 74 (1998)

questions.prompt: Francisco Suárez, a 16th-century Jesuit, produced a later, highly influential synthesis often called Suarezian scholasticism -- distinct from strict Thomism on several metaphysical questions, including the real distinction between essence and existence. What does the Church's acceptance of a THIRD major school, centuries after Aquinas and Scotus, show about how 'schools of Catholic philosophy' actually work?
choices: The list of legitimate Catholic philosophical schools was never permanently closed at two -- new syntheses can be received into the tradition as genuinely Catholic so long as they remain compatible with revealed doctrine, not fixed forever at whichever schools existed first
Suárez's work was rejected by the Church as incompatible with Catholic teaching
Only philosophers who lived before the Reformation can found a legitimate Catholic school
The Church requires all three schools to be taught as one single unified system
questions.correctAnswer: The list of legitimate Catholic philosophical schools was never permanently closed at two -- new syntheses can be received into the tradition as genuinely Catholic so long as they remain compatible with revealed doctrine, not fixed forever at whichever schools existed first
questions.explanation: Suárez shows this isn't a closed, ancient list -- the Church's philosophical tradition keeps developing new syntheses, provided they serve rather than contradict revealed truth. This is the same distinction Heresies (level 8) drew against Modernism: development of a school of thought's tools is not the same error as claiming revealed dogma itself changes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the Church has ever formally closed the list of acceptable schools, or whether new ones keep being received.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, n. 62 (1998)

questions.prompt: Fides et Ratio famously opens by calling faith and reason 'like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth.' What two errors does the encyclical warn against in describing their relationship?
choices: Fideism (faith alone, distrusting or bypassing reason) and rationalism (reason alone, refusing anything reason cannot independently verify) -- each severs one wing and calls the result flight
Only Modernism is warned against; reason is treated as entirely reliable on its own
Only rationalism is warned against; the encyclical has no concerns about fideism
Scholasticism and Neo-Platonism are the two errors named
questions.correctAnswer: Fideism (faith alone, distrusting or bypassing reason) and rationalism (reason alone, refusing anything reason cannot independently verify) -- each severs one wing and calls the result flight
questions.explanation: The 'two wings' image only works if both are actually needed -- the encyclical spends real space warning against fideism (which makes faith irrational, needing no reasoned support at all) and rationalism (which treats unaided human reason as needing nothing beyond itself), naming both as failures to keep faith and reason working together as this whole topic has been arguing they should.
questions.hint: The metaphor needs both wings -- ask what happens, and what each failure is called, when you try to fly with only one.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, Prologue and n. 52-55 (1998)

questions.prompt: True or false: because the Church tolerates multiple philosophical schools, she therefore has no philosophical positions at all that a Catholic thinker cannot deny.
questions.explanation: Fides et Ratio is explicit that some principles -- the reality of truth, the human capacity to know it, the existence of a real created order distinct from God -- are not optional philosophical opinions a Catholic thinker may simply reject, even while real diversity remains on how best to explain and systematize those shared commitments. Pluralism operates inside a real boundary, not in place of one.
questions.hint: Pluralism among schools that all still affirm certain basics is different from having no boundaries at all.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, n. 4-6 (1998)

questions.prompt: Match each philosopher or school to its distinctive position.

pairs.right: Being is said of God and creatures analogically, not univocally
Being is said univocally of God and creatures
Divine illumination is needed for the mind to grasp unchanging truth
A later synthesis proposing its own account of essence and existence

questions.explanation: None of these four disagreements makes any of these four thinkers heretical -- all four are honored figures within the Catholic philosophical tradition, disagreeing on real metaphysical questions while affirming the same revealed truths those questions serve.
questions.hint: Each of these four holds a distinctive, real position on a shared metaphysical question -- none of the four positions is a doctrinal error.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, n. 44, 62, 74 (1998)

questions.prompt: This entire topic has moved from 'Being and Reason' (level 1) through act and potency, causality, the transcendentals, natural theology, essence and existence, angelic natures, and finally to the schools that have argued over how best to explain all of it. What is Fides et Ratio's own summary of philosophy's proper relationship to theology, which this whole arc has been building toward?
choices: Philosophy is not a rival to theology or a replacement for revelation, but a genuine, necessary partner -- reason has real, proper work to do in understanding what faith already holds to be true, without either side swallowing the other
Philosophy should be abandoned entirely in favor of faith alone
Theology is merely philosophy with religious language added on top, with no distinct subject matter of its own
Philosophy and theology have no relationship to each other and should be studied in total isolation
questions.correctAnswer: Philosophy is not a rival to theology or a replacement for revelation, but a genuine, necessary partner -- reason has real, proper work to do in understanding what faith already holds to be true, without either side swallowing the other
questions.explanation: This is the whole point of ending the topic here: every metaphysical tool this topic built -- act and potency, causality, the transcendentals, angelic natures -- exists to help reason do real work alongside faith, not to replace it or be replaced by it. The schools disagree on method and detail; none of them, rightly practiced, treats philosophy as faith's rival.
questions.hint: This is the encyclical's own answer to why philosophy matters to a believer at all -- not as a rival to faith, but genuine partner work.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, Prologue (1998)

questions.prompt: A student objects: 'if even Aquinas and Scotus disagree on something as basic as how being applies to God, doesn't that mean metaphysics is just opinion, with nothing objectively knowable at all?' What is the accurate response, per everything this topic has covered?
choices: No -- both thinkers agree that being, causality, and objective truth are real and knowable; they disagree on the best technical account of how analogy or univocity precisely works, which is a narrower, genuine dispute inside a much larger shared realism, not evidence that nothing is knowable at all
Yes -- this disagreement proves that all metaphysical claims are equally arbitrary
The disagreement proves the Church has no coherent view of God whatsoever
Only one of the two men can be considered a real philosopher at all
questions.correctAnswer: No -- both thinkers agree that being, causality, and objective truth are real and knowable; they disagree on the best technical account of how analogy or univocity precisely works, which is a narrower, genuine dispute inside a much larger shared realism, not evidence that nothing is knowable at all
questions.explanation: This is the correct final move for anyone using this material apologetically: pointing to real disagreement among serious thinkers to conclude 'therefore nothing is really knowable' is a non sequitur. Genuine, bounded disagreement about technical details is entirely compatible with -- and, if anything, presupposes -- a much larger shared confidence that being, truth, and causality are real and available to reason in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask how much these two thinkers actually agree on before getting to the point where they disagree.

citations.reference: John Paul II, Fides et Ratio, n. 4-6, 44 (1998)
